And if he produces it, and so forth. This law requires clarification. Suppose Reuven deposited one hundred with Shimon as a third party to give to Levi, and Shimon delivered it to Levi in accordance with the entrustment. Reuven now challenges Levi. Is Shimon still believed like two witnesses in Levi's favor, or do we say that once the deposited item has left Shimon's hands, he loses all special credibility and becomes like any ordinary witness? Rashba, in his chiddushim to Gittin 64b, cites Raavad that an ordinary third party remains believed in favor of the person to whom he delivered the item even though the item is no longer in his own hands, because he could have returned it to that recipient while it was still under his control. Rashba gives another reason. Once he delivered the item, at the moment of delivery he had full third-party credibility. Therefore, even if he did not deliver it before witnesses, the recipient's present possession itself proves that the third party handed it to him in the claimed legal capacity. We effectively have testimony from the very fact of possession that the third party acted properly. Rashba then explains the contrary rule that "when the third-party matter is no longer in his possession, he is not believed." That applies where the third party now testifies against the person to whom he delivered it. For example, he gave the item to Levi and later says, "My delivery was subject to a condition," while Levi denies that condition. Since Levi is now in possession, the third party has no special power to remove it from him; at most he is like an ordinary single witness. The same is true where it is known that Levi took the item without the third party's consent. Thus, where Shimon delivered to Levi and afterward testifies in Levi's favor that the delivery was proper, his statement is treated as if the deposited item were still in his own hands. Maharam in Mordechai, Perek HaMekabel, and Responsa Maimoniyot, Sefer Mishpatim, siman 44, say similarly. A third party remains believed concerning what he did while the entrusted item was in his hands even if it is no longer there. We presume he carried out his agency properly, because an agent is presumed to perform his mission and we do not assume he changed instructions merely in order to sin without personal benefit. The Tosefta saying that a third party is not believed once the item is no longer in his possession concerns a later dispute about what the original conditions had been. After time has passed, he may not remember precise old terms. But he is believed retrospectively to say, "What I did while it was in my hands was done lawfully," because at that time the matter was immediately before him and he was careful to act correctly. Hagahot Mordechai in Perek HaMekabel asks from the baraita in Perek Zeh Borer, "If there are no witnesses on it and it comes from the hand of a third party," which sounds as though the item must still be physically in the third party's hand. It answers that the same law applies even after the item has left his hand. The baraita's formulation was needed only for the later clause teaching the additional case where the receipt appears after the signatures of the note. Agudah likewise writes explicitly that the third party remains believed after the item has left his hand. Their intent is plainly the same as Rashba's: he remains believed in favor of Levi, to whom he delivered the object. Against Levi he is no longer believed once Levi possesses it and denies the alleged limitation. Rambam, Hilchot Gerushin 12:11, is also explicit. If a get is in the woman's hand and she says, "This agent gave it to me," and the agent says, "Yes, I gave it to her, and the husband gave it to me for divorce," while the husband says, "I gave it to him merely for safekeeping," the agent is believed and the woman is divorced. Shulchan Aruch in Even HaEzer siman 141, seif 56, cites this without qualification. Thus, even though the get is now in the woman's hand and no longer in the third party's hand, the agent is believed regarding the lawful character of his prior delivery. Rambam rules like R. Chisda; all the more so in monetary matters, where even R. Huna generally concedes that rights can be waived. Rif also appears to support this. He explains "the husband says deposit and the third party says divorce" as referring to a delivery agent. The get must already be in the woman's hand, because otherwise the husband can simply revoke the agency. Yet R. Chisda says the third party is believed. It would be strained to say the case is specifically one where the third party first announced before witnesses, while the get was still in his hand, that he held it for divorce and only then delivered it. The Gemara states the matter generally, without such a qualification. Maharsha explains why Tosafot preferred to interpret "third party says divorce" as an acceptance agent rather than as a delivery agent: once the get has left the third party's possession, he may no longer be believed. At first glance Maharsha's statement is difficult, because Tosafot elsewhere say that the agents who require saying "it was written and signed before me" are not troubled by the husband's later claim that the get was merely deposited, since they follow R. Chisda that the third party is believed. But there the get is obviously already in the woman's hand. The resolution is that the Gemara's unqualified statement could include cases where no witnesses heard the third party declare the nature of the entrustment before delivery. Tosafot did not want to explain the core dispute through a delivery agent because the question whether he remains believed after delivery is itself not simple according to all views. In the Diaspora agency case, however, the woman necessarily proves that the agent made the required declaration before beit din, "it was written and signed before me." That declaration itself is made before final delivery and thus records his account of the entrustment while he still functions as agent. Once the woman establishes that, the later husband's denial is weaker. Therefore Tosafot can rely on R. Chisda there even if they hesitate about the unqualified general case. Nevertheless, Maharsha's reading is not compelled. Rambam clearly holds that even after delivery the third party remains believed. He still interprets the Gemara's case as an acceptance agent, as Maggid Mishneh explains. There can be other reasons for that interpretation. Ran offers another distinction. R. Huna's "if it were so" argument depends on the assumption that an agent for receipt should have immediately completed the divorce rather than keep the get. In a delivery agency, once the agent delivered the get to the woman, he did exactly what he was supposed to do. Therefore the "if it were so" reasoning is weaker. Under this distinction, after a delivery agent completes delivery he can remain believed even though the item has left his hands. This provides another answer to Maharsha. Tur in Even HaEzer siman 141, citing Rambam, also understands the rule that even when the get is in the woman's hand the agent can be believed. There is therefore significant support for applying the same principle in monetary law. We find a possible dissent in Mordechai, Perek Sheni of Kiddushin, and Hagahot Maimoniyot, Hilchot Ishut chapter 3. They say that an agent for delivery in kiddushin or divorce does not need written authorization or witnesses, but if the principal later denies the agency after the kiddushin money or get has been delivered, the result is doubtful and we rule stringently, because the entrusted item is no longer in the agent's hands. Shulchan Aruch cites this in Even HaEzer siman 141, seif 11. This can be limited. It may concern a case where there are no witnesses before us showing that the agent delivered the item as the principal's agent. If witnesses had heard his declaration while the item was still in his hand, then the rule would be like a third party who stated the terms of the entrustment before delivery, and his statement would stand. In kiddushin by money, witnesses are of course needed to see the money given for kiddushin. Yet even there, the difficulty is not only whether the agent delivered but whether the principal appointed him to effect kiddushin. Mere possession of another person's money does not prove he was authorized to marry a woman on that person's behalf. This explains why the issue can be doubtful even while the money once stood in his hand. I have discussed this elsewhere in my chiddushim to Even HaEzer. One can also explain Mordechai and Hagahot Maimoniyot like Raavad. Their reason for believing a third party after delivery is that the recipient could return the item to him, thereby restoring his control. That logic fits an acceptance agent: if the woman returns the get to the agent, his possession again carries third-party force. It is weaker for a delivery agent. If the woman returns the get to him, the husband can immediately revoke his agency; the return itself may defeat the supposed completed delivery. Thus the phrase "the third-party matter is no longer in his hand" has special significance with delivery agency. This also reconciles Shulchan Aruch's two rulings. In seif 11 he cites Hagahot Maimoniyot that the husband can deny a delivery agency after the item has left the agent's hand. In seifim 55 and 56 he follows Rambam that an acceptance agent remains believed even when the get is in the woman's hand. These need not conflict. The latter case concerns an agent for receipt, where the woman's hand can be treated as the agent's continuing legal hand and the husband has no power to revoke after receipt. The former concerns an agent for delivery, where returning the get to the agent would simply restore the husband's power of revocation. This may also be what Maharsha intended in reading Tosafot. When Tosafot say "the third party says for divorce," they choose an acceptance agent because in that case even after the get reaches the woman the third party retains legal credibility. A delivery agent is more problematic once actual delivery has ended. Rama's gloss in Even HaEzer, seifim 55 and 57, appears to understand Rosh as holding more broadly that once the third-party item has left the agent's hands he is no longer believed. Beit Shmuel, seif katan 79, correctly objects that Rama's proof from Tur is not decisive. Yet Rosh's commentary to Gittin does contain language supporting Rama. Rosh asks on the Gemara's statement "R. Huna concedes if the woman says it was given to him before me": how is that similar to the earlier dispute, where the get is in the third party's hand, while here it is in the woman's hand? From this he derives that even if the get is still in the third party's hand the woman can possess a migo. The question appears to assume that if the get were already in the woman's hand, the ordinary third-party rule would not automatically apply. Beit Shmuel tries to answer that Rosh may follow Ran that once the get is in the woman's hand the "if it were so" argument no longer applies, so even R. Huna would believe the third party. I do not find this compelling. The mishnah there concerns the period of persecution, when after the divorce the get was immediately torn to avoid danger from the government. If the reason were that an acceptance agent should have handed the get immediately to the woman, there was no time to do so: once he received it, the marriage ended and the document had to be destroyed for safety. Handing the torn pieces to the woman would provide her no meaningful proof or benefit. Rosh would have said this explicitly if it were his point. Still, Rosh's language can be understood more narrowly. Since R. Huna and R. Chisda dispute the rule generally even while the get remains in the third party's hand, the Gemara's later unqualified statement should likewise naturally concern the same factual setting unless it specifies otherwise. Rosh's question may therefore be merely textual: if the later case works only where the get is in the woman's hand, the Gemara should have said so expressly. This does not prove Rosh believes the agent is never trusted after delivery. I once suggested another approach in my chiddushim. Rosh may hold that where the agent says, "I am a delivery agent," even R. Huna concedes he is believed because the "if it were so" argument is weak: the get may have been written on an earlier date, and if directly delivered later it could be considered antedated, whereas delivery through an agent creates publicity and avoids the problem. Therefore, the agent could have a migo to say he was an acceptance agent. But this does not fit Tur's language that in one city one should not appoint a delivery agent because the husband may later say it was merely a deposit. I leave the point with the qualification noted above. Even if Rama's reading of Rosh is accepted for gittin, it need not govern monetary law. Maharam, Rosh's teacher, says explicitly in Mordechai that in monetary cases we presume an agent performed his mission and the burden of proof lies on the claimant who seeks to undo the recipient's possession. With a get, where the issue is a possible prohibition of a married woman, doubt is treated stringently. Thus Rosh can be stricter in gittin while accepting Maharam's monetary rule. The same distinction can explain Hagahot Maimoniyot. Raavyah, who in one case rules there is no kiddushin at all, may follow Raavad's different rationale; but in monetary law the weight of authority supports continued credibility. Therefore, in monetary matters I do not find a genuine dispute: once the third party lawfully delivered the item to Levi and later testifies in Levi's favor concerning what he did while the item was under his control, he is believed as though the item were still in his hand. Against Levi, however, once Levi possesses the item and contradicts him, the third party is only like an ordinary witness.
It appears further that Raavad, Rashba, and Maharam needed their special reasons only where Levi himself does not claim with certainty that the item belongs to him and relies solely on the third party's statement, as in a get where the woman does not know whether the husband delivered it for safekeeping or divorce. If Levi himself says with certainty, "The money belongs to me under the terms of the entrustment," there should be no doubt at all. The entire basis of third-party credibility is that the depositor trusted the holder. The owner knew that the third party might breach the deposit and hand the item to the other litigant. By entrusting him, the owner accepted that if the holder did so, the recipient could rely on that act. Once the third party has actually delivered the item, this is precisely the risk the depositor knowingly accepted. Why should the recipient's position become weaker merely because delivery has already taken place? The special reasons were needed only where the recipient lacks independent knowledge. One might then say that the owner trusted the third party only against the possibility that he would physically deliver the item, but did not accept that the recipient could later rely on the third party's verbal explanation after the fact. In such a case we need Raavad's power-to-return rationale, Rashba's possession-as-proof rationale, or Maharam's presumption that an agent performs his mission. The same is true of migo. If Levi has a migo, he can say, "When the third party delivered the item, he expressly told me the terms were such-and-such." If a statement by the third party made before witnesses at the time of delivery would be effective, Levi's migo gives him the same force. Therefore the uncertainty discussed by the authorities is principally a case where the recipient cannot independently assert the relevant facts. This is simple and correct.
But if there is a grievance against him, and so forth. Shach, seif katan 20, explains that "grievance" here does not mean the parties dispute how much property was deposited, as Mechaber discussed at the beginning of seif 1. Rather, following R. Yehudah Albargeloni, it means that the owner says to the third party, "You wrongfully delivered my deposit to Levi." Even if the item were still in the third party's hand and he said in beit din that according to the terms of the entrustment it belongs to Levi, beit din would direct him to give it to Levi and he would owe no oath, because he has no personal stake in whether Levi receives it. But once he has already handed it over, the owner can make him swear that he did not violate the entrustment. He then becomes a witness who himself must take an oath and can no longer testify. According to what I established above, however, once the third party delivered the item to Levi and afterward testifies in Levi's favor, the situation is legally like one where the item remains in the third party's own hand. Levi's position cannot become worse because the third party already performed the delivery. If so, the entire explanation collapses. The rule in Shulchan Aruch that, once the item has left the third party's hand, he is only like one witness must concern testimony against Levi. In that situation, why should a grievance by the owner prevent him from testifying against Levi? If anything, the alleged misconduct involved favoring Levi, not harming him. Shach writes that even Rashba agrees that if the owner has a grievance that the third party delivered improperly, the third party becomes interested and cannot testify even in Levi's favor. I do not find this correct. Rashba's reason is that the recipient's possession itself proves that the third party delivered in the claimed legal manner, as though he had done so before witnesses. If there had actually been witnesses to the delivery, would the owner's later grievance make the third party "interested" and destroy what those witnesses saw? Certainly not. The same should follow from Rashba's reasoning. One could force a different case. Shimon delivered the item to Levi but now testifies that the delivery was subject to a condition containing asmachta or some other invalid clause, such that on Shimon's present version Levi must return the item to Reuven. Reuven meanwhile accuses Shimon of having delivered the deposit wrongfully and demands an oath. Shimon now has an interest in testifying against Levi: if he does not say the condition was invalid and that Levi must return the property, Shimon may remain exposed to Reuven's oath claim. By testifying against Levi, he can cause the item to return to Reuven and thereby neutralize Reuven's grievance. But this is strained, and in any event the underlying law requiring the oath is itself doubtful. If the third party would have been believed without an oath while the item was still in his hand because we say, "Why should he sin for no benefit," why should he suddenly become obligated to swear merely because he carried out the entrusted act without first consulting beit din? If he asks beit din what to do, they tell him, "Give the item to Levi; you need no oath." If he does exactly the same thing on his own, in accordance with his duty as third party, why should he now owe an oath? What difference does it make whether he delivered in the presence of beit din or before witnesses? Shach himself recognizes that if he delivered before witnesses he is believed. But why should the presence of witnesses affect whether the owner can impose an oath? The third party's conduct was the same. Rav Hai Gaon infers from R. Nachman's statement that he "believed" the elderly woman that she was believed without an oath. Shach elsewhere accepts that many authorities, including Mordechai, Hagahot Mordechai, Responsa Maimoniyot, and Agudah, exempt a third party from an oath. He nevertheless prefers R. Yehudah Albargeloni because Baal HaTerumot, Baal HaIttur, Tur, and Mechaber cite him. But R. Yehudah Albargeloni never meant what Shach attributes to him. Baal HaTerumot, Shaar 52, part 3, letter 1, cites Baal HaIttur in his name. Later, letter 7 of the same section says: "Although some authorities wrote that if the litigants have a grievance against the third party regarding the matter of his entrustment, even after it has left his hand he is considered interested and is not believed..." This is plainly the same R. Yehudah Albargeloni, since no other authority is cited with that exact "grievance" language. Baal HaTerumot immediately explains: "These words of the Geonim were said only where there is a dispute between them, he says you deposited only so much and they each say there was more in his hand." Thus Baal HaTerumot himself explains "grievance" as a dispute over the quantity or amount deposited, exactly as I have written. The words "even after it left his hand" likewise imply the same rule would apply before it left his hand if the monetary dispute existed. That makes sense if the parties dispute the amount of the entrusted property. It does not fit Shach's theory that the oath arises only because he already delivered the item. Maharit, cited by Shach, likewise interprets the phrase as a dispute over the amount of the deposited property. This is therefore the correct reading, supported by both Baal HaTerumot and Maharit. There is no reason to invent a dispute among the authorities where Mordechai, Agudah, and Responsa Maimoniyot exempt the third party from oath and only one line is forced against them. Shach's only significant proof is Responsa Rosh, klal 105, siman 3, where Dona Velidira was required to swear that she returned the note to Dona Lidisia lawfully. Rosh says she cannot be exempted merely because a third party is normally believed, because the entrusted matter is no longer in her possession. This seems to distinguish precisely between before and after delivery. Even if Rosh holds this, he stands alone against the many authorities cited above. Moreover, the case itself has an additional feature. The claimant's representative apparently knew the underlying facts independently, as can be inferred from the responsum. If so, his testimony functioned as one witness against Dona Velidira, requiring a Torah oath, not merely the rabbinic oath. This explains Rosh's phrase that she must take a Torah oath. Otherwise, why would the case involve anything more than a rabbinic oath over an alleged breach of deposit? Once there is a single opposing witness, the matter is different. The presumption that an agent performs his agency can support leniency concerning a rabbinic oath and prevent Chazal from imposing routine oaths on trusted third parties. It cannot override a Torah oath triggered by an actual witness. Likewise, the policy reason not to discourage people from serving as third parties applies to rabbinic enactments, not to a Torah oath. Rosh's case can therefore be fully reconciled with the majority view. There is a second possible distinction. Perhaps Rosh holds that while the third-party item remains intact in the holder's hand, his special credibility is as strong as possession itself. In the Dona Velidira case the original note had already been returned and could not be restored to the holder. The special possession basis was therefore gone. Yet even this does not establish Shach's broad oath rule. In any event, we should not extend Rosh beyond necessity. The proper practical rule is that an ordinary third party who acts according to his entrusted instructions is not required to take a rabbinic oath merely because the owner later complains that he delivered improperly. The authorities explicitly exempt him, and imposing such an oath would undermine the entire institution of third-party entrustment: no one would agree to serve if every later dissatisfied litigant could force him to swear. Where the litigants dispute the amount of the entrusted property, however, there is a true personal monetary controversy involving the third party. He may then be considered interested concerning that disputed portion, as R. Yehudah Albargeloni, Baal HaTerumot, and Maharit state. And where a Torah oath arises through an actual opposing witness, the third party must swear. That is a separate rule. Thus Sema's interpretation is correct, and Bach's distinction above is also correct: the principal difficulty concerns a person who denies the third-party arrangement itself. Shach's extension of the grievance rule to ordinary delivery against an owner's later complaint should not be accepted.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
לא יהיה נאמן כו' עיין תומים שהארכתי ובררתי מילתא בטעמא כי העיקר כדברי רשב"א דאם ראובן השליש ביד שמעון ושמעון מסרו ללוי לטובת לוי יכול להעיד אפי' דהשלישית ביד לוי דלא גרע זכות לוי מאלו היה ביד שמעון השליש אבל להעיד לחובת לוי אינו נאמן דלוי אומר לאו כל כמיניה כיון דתו ליכא שלישית בידו כלל וגם אם נחלקו בתנאים שהיה ביניהם מעיקרא שאין ענין למסירת השלישי' בהא אמרינן כיון דלא רמיא אנפשיה לא מדכר כולי האי ודי דהוי כע"א גם אם יש ללוי מגו ג"כ נאמן דשליש מסרו בתנאי' הללו כמו דמסרו בעדים דמ"ש כיון דיש לו מגו ה"ל כמסרו בעדים ואנן סהדי ומכ"ש בטוען ברי מפי עצמו וכל הנ"ל מיירי דאין לו שום טענת ברי כלל רק מפי שליש מכל מקום לטובת לוי יכול להעיד וזה מבואר הכל שם וע"ש שהארכתי:
ואין להם תרעומת עיין בתומים דבררתי דלא כש"ך דכתב דאם מסר שמעון שלישית ללוי יכול ראובן להשביע שלא עשה נגד שלישתו דזה אינו דאין כאן שבועה כלל על השליש דחזקה אין אדם חוטא ולא לו אם לא במקום שע"א מכחישו בזו י"ל דעת הרא"ש דחייב שבועה אבל היסת ליכא:
אבל אם יש להם תרעומת פי' הסמ"ע דהיינו דמחולק' בסכום שלישית זה אומר ק' והשליש אומר רק פ' ואף דכבר מבואר כן בריש סימן נאמר שני' פה דשם איירי לענין נאמנות כשנים וכאן לענין ע"א סמ"ע והב"ח תי' דלעיל בשלישית בידו אף דהוי הכחשה בסך מכל מקום אם מודה בשלישית נאמן וכאן אפילו מודה בשלישית אבל בשלישות בידו ומודה בשלישות אף דהוי הכחשה בסך מכל מקום פטור משבועה ובזה השיגו הש"ך והנכון אתו דמכל מקום חייב שבועה אבל לדינא הסכמתי דאף דצריך שבועה מ"מ נאמן בשבועה כמש"ל בסעיף א' משא"כ באין שלישות בידו והוי הכחשה בסך אינו נאמן כע"א כלל:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
He will not be believed, etc. See Tumim, where I discussed this at length and established the reason. The principal rule is like Rashba. If Reuven deposited a matter with Shimon, and Shimon later delivered it to Levi for Levi's benefit, Shimon may still testify in Levi's favor even though the deposited item is now in Levi's possession, because Levi's right is no weaker than it would have been while the item remained with Shimon. But Shimon is not believed to testify against Levi, because Levi can say, "You no longer have any authority over me, since the deposited matter is no longer in your possession at all." Likewise, where they dispute the original conditions between them and the later delivery has no bearing on those conditions, we say that because the matter was not incumbent on him to remember, he may not remember it accurately, and at most he is like one witness. If Levi has a migo, however, he too is believed that the third party delivered it under those conditions, just as if the delivery had occurred before witnesses. Since he has a migo, it is as though the delivery was witnessed. Certainly this is so where Levi himself makes a definite claim. All of the foregoing concerns a case where Levi has no definite claim of his own and relies solely on the third party, yet the third party can still testify in Levi's favor. All this is explained there at length.
And they have no grievance. See Tumim, where I established against Shach that if Shimon delivered the deposited matter to Levi, Reuven cannot impose an oath on Shimon that he did not act contrary to the terms of the deposit. There is no oath at all upon the third party, because a person is presumed not to sin for no personal gain. Only where one witness contradicts him may it be possible, according to Rosh, that he must swear. But there is no hesset oath.
But if they have a grievance. Sema explains that they dispute the amount of the deposit, one saying it was one hundred and the third party saying it was only eighty. Although this was already stated at the beginning of the siman, it is repeated there regarding the third party's credibility as equivalent to two witnesses, whereas here it concerns his status as one witness, Sema. Bach answers that above, where the deposited matter remains in his possession and he admits the fact of the deposit, even though they dispute the amount, he remains believed. Here, even if he admits the deposit, because it is no longer in his possession and they dispute the amount, his status is different. Shach objects to the suggestion that while the deposit remains with him he would be exempt from an oath despite a dispute over the amount, and Shach is correct, for he must swear. As practical law, however, I concluded that although he must swear, he remains believed with that oath as I wrote above in seif 1. By contrast, where the deposited matter is no longer in his possession and they dispute the amount, he is not believed even as one witness.

mechaber.he: שטר שיוצא מת"י שליש והלוה טוען שהוא מזוייף או פרוע אם אין יכולין לקיים חתימת העדים אע"פ שהשליש מעיד שהמלוה והלוה מסרוהו לו ואמרו לו שכך וכך נשאר עדיין לפרוע משטר זה אינו נאמן:
mechaber.en: A third-year-old note that he is fake or wild if he is unable to fulfill the signature of witnesses that the third indicates that the loan and the loan have been told and told him that so and so remains to break this regime is not true:

baer_hetev.he: פרוע. כת' הש"ך דהנ"י חולק ע"ז דאם טוען פרוע כיון שהשליש הי' יכול לקיימו בשום פעם אע"פ שאין יכול לקיימו עכשיו נאמן השליש ע"כ מיהו אם טוען הלו' מזויף כ"ע מודו דאין השליש נאמן עכ"ל:
baer_hetev.en: Paid. The Shach writes that Nimukei Yosef disagrees with this ruling. If the borrower claims that the document was paid, then because the third party could at some earlier time have authenticated the document, he is believed even though he can no longer authenticate it now. If, however, the borrower claims that the document is forged, all agree that the third party is not believed. Thus concludes the Shach.

beer_hagolah.he:
ס) שם סעיף א':
ע) ומפרש שם הטעם שאין השליש נאמן יותר מבעל דבר בעצמו ואילו היה השטר ביד המלוה כיון שאינו יכול לקיימו אינו כלום ומבואר לעיל ריש סי' מ"ו וכתב הב"ח ☜ודאי דלא גרע מע"א ומזקיקו לידי ש"ד וכדין שליש שאין שלישותו בידו דהכא נמי לאו מידי בידו אלא מספק בעלמא ולא מצי טעין הכא השטאה או שלא להשביע כיון ששניהם מודים שעשאוהו שליש וכו' ושראה כתיבת יד מהרש"ל שהי' מסתפק בדבר ושנלע"ד אין כאן ספק דפשיטא שחייב ש"ד והכי נקטינן ודלא כהסמ"ע עכ"ל
beer_hagolah.en:
s) There, seif 1.
o) The reason explained there is that the third party is not more credible than the litigant himself. If the document were in the lender's possession, since he could not validate it, it would have no effect, as explained above at the beginning of siman 46. The Bach writes that certainly it is no worse than one witness and therefore requires a Torah oath, like a third party whose entrusted item is no longer in his possession. Here too he has nothing in his possession and there is only uncertainty. The debtor cannot claim jesting or that the admission was made to avoid appearing wealthy, because both parties admit that they appointed him as third party, etc. The Bach writes that he saw Maharshal's handwriting expressing doubt about the matter, but in his view there is no doubt: it is obvious that a Torah oath is required, and this is the practical ruling, unlike the Sema.

beur_hagra.he: שטר שיוצא. גטין שם מי קנפיק כו' וערש"י שם אבל זה שקרעו כו' יה"ה כאן:
beur_hagra.en: A document produced from. See Gittin there: 'From whose possession did it emerge, etc.?' See Rashi, who explains that the one who tore it acted falsely. The same applies here.

chelkat_mechokek.he: או שפירסה נידה. אין חילוק בין שעת וסתה לשלא בשעת וסתה ולא מצי אמרה נסתחפ' שדיהו דהא אפי' בחלה הוא וחלת' היא הוי אונס ולא נזכר בגמרא בכתובות דף ב' ע"א חילוק זה אלא באת"ל חלה הוא או היא מעלה לה מזונות ועוד אכתוב מזה לקמן בסי' ס' ס"ק א' ועיין שם:
chelkat_mechokek.en: Or she became a niddah. There is no distinction between this occurring at her expected menstrual period and outside that period. She cannot say, "his field was stricken by misfortune," for even if he became ill or she became ill, it is an unavoidable circumstance. The Gemara in Ketubot 2a mentions such a distinction only within the conditional discussion whether, if he or she became ill, he must provide her support. I will discuss this further below, siman 60, seif katan 1; see there.

haggahot_imrei_barukh.he: (נה"מ הנ"ל) על תנאי כך וכך כו'. נ"ב צ"ע כיון שיודע השליש שקיים הלוה התנאי הרי השטר כפרוע ובידו שלא להחזיר ליד המלוה כ"א למסור להלוה וכמו כן היכא שהיה על המלוה לקיים דבר וכשלא יקיים יהיה השטר בטל וידוע שעבר המלוה על התנאי כדאיתא בסמ"ע:
haggahot_imrei_barukh.en: (Netivot HaMishpat, there) On condition of such and such, etc. Note: This requires study. Since the third party knows that the debtor fulfilled the condition, the document is effectively paid, and he has the ability not to return it to the lender but to deliver it to the debtor. The same applies where the lender had to perform something, with the document to be void if he failed, and it is known that the lender violated the condition, as stated in the Sema.

ketzot_hachoshen.he: אין יכולים לקיים. והיינו כיון דאין יכולין לקיים תו לית לי' לשליש מגו דאי בעי מהדר לי' ללוה דהא אי נמי מהדר לי' אינו מועיל כיון דאינו יכול לקיימו ועיין ש"ך הביא בשם הנימוקי שחולק וס"ל דאם טוען פרוע כיון שהי' השליש יכול לקיימו בשום פעם אף על גב שאין יכול לקיים עכשיו נאמן השליש ועיין ש"ך בסק"א האריך והעלה בזה דאם אומר מזוייף אם כן לא הימני' מעולם כיון דלפי דבריו לא יוכל לקיימו בשום פעם אבל כשמודה שכתבו הרי מודה שהי' שליש והי' יכול לקיימו בשום זמן והימני' לשליש ועיין שם ואכתי צריך עיון כיון דע"כ נאמנות דשליש אינו כשני עדים דהא אם באו עדים והכחישו עדים נאמנים יותר וכיון דלא הוי שליש אלא כמו נאמנות סתם נהי שמודה שהוא שליש ניהימני' ללוה לומר פרוע במגו דהי' טוען מזוייף וכ"כ בשלחן ערוך סימן עיין בשטר שיש נאמנות ועיין שם בדברי הסמ"ע והש"ך ולכל הפירושי' בנאמנות סתם ואין עדים על הנאמנות אלא שהלוה מודה נאמן במגו נגד נאמנות וה"נ נהי דשליש נאמנות יש לו כיון דאין עדי' שהאמינו דהא אינו מקויים אם כן ליהמני' במגו דלא האמינו כלל דאומר מזויף אין כאן נאמנות וכ"כ בשלחן ערוך סימן מ"ו בשטר שאינו מקויים ואפילו כתוב בו נאמנות נאמן במגו דמזויף ולכן יראה דהנימוקי ס"ל דלא מהני מגו דמזויף בנאמנת וכדעת בעל התרומות ועיין שם שני דיעות בשלחן ערוך סימן מ"ו סעי' ב' אבל לפי מה דקיימא לן דנאמן לומר פרוע בשטר שאינו מקויים אפילו כתוב בו נאמנות אם כן הוא הדין נגד נאמנות דשליש נאמן במגו:
ketzot_hachoshen.en: They cannot validate it. The reason is that if the document cannot now be validated, the shalish no longer has the migo that he could simply return it to the borrower. Returning it would accomplish nothing when the instrument itself cannot be established. The Shach cites Nimukei Yosef as disagreeing where the shalish says the document was paid. Since there was a time when the shalish could have validated or returned the document effectively, his credibility once arose and does not disappear merely because he cannot validate it now. The Shach distinguishes: if the borrower claims the document is forged, then according to his own words the shalish could never have validated it and therefore was never entrusted through a valid migo. But if the borrower admits he wrote it and merely claims payment, he thereby admits that the shalish once had a valid position from which he could have validated or returned it, and therefore the shalish remains believed. This still requires study. The credibility of a shalish is not literally the force of two witnesses, because if actual witnesses contradict him, the witnesses prevail. It is closer to an agreed credibility clause. If the instrument itself is not validated and the only basis for saying the shalish was trusted comes from the borrower's own admission, why should the borrower not be believed through a migo that he could have said the document was forged and that the shalish was never trusted at all? With an ordinary contractual credibility clause contained in an unvalidated document, the borrower is believed through a migo of forgery to say the debt was paid, despite the credibility clause. The same should apply to the shalish. The Nimukei Yosef can be sustained only according to the authorities who do not allow a migo of forgery to overcome a credibility clause, as Baal HaTerumot holds and as reflected in one opinion in siman 46. According to our practical law, however, which permits a payment claim against an unvalidated document even where it contains a general credibility clause because of the migo of forgery, the borrower should likewise be believed against the shalish's special credibility. Therefore the Shach's distinction cannot be universally accepted.

meirat_einayim.he: אינו נאמן. ז"ל הטור שאין השליש נאמן בתפיסתו יותר מבע"ד עצמי ואלו היה השטר ביד המלוה כיון שאינו יכול לקיימו אינו כלום שמודה בשטר שכתבו צריך לקיימו ואין כח ביד השליש לעשות משטר מזויף כשר עכ"ל ועפ"ר שם כתבתי בשם מור"ש ז"ל אפי' שבועה דאוריי' אינו מחויב השליש לשכנגדו על מה שאומר שהודה בפניו שח"ל כך וכך בשטר זה אם לא אמרו לו בתחלה אתה תהיה עד בדבר [דאם א"ל כן מתחלה היה צריך שבועה כעד א' וכמ"ש הטור והמחבר בסימן פ"א ס"י] דיכול לומר משטה הייתי בך או שלא להשביע אמרתי כן עמ"ש שם עוד מזה:
meirat_einayim.en: He is not believed. The Tur explains that the custodian's possession gives him no greater credibility than the litigant himself. If the document were in the lender's hand and could not be authenticated, it would be worthless, because one who admits that he wrote a document must still authenticate it. The custodian cannot transform a forged or unauthenticated document into a valid one merely through his own statement. In Perishah I cited Maharshal that the custodian is not even liable to take a Torah oath against the opposing party based on his claim that the latter admitted before him that he owed the amount in the document, unless the parties originally said to him, 'You shall be a witness to this matter.' If they did so, he would have the law of one witness and an oath would be required, as explained in siman 81:10. Otherwise the opposing party can say, 'I was joking with you,' or 'I said it so as not to appear wealthy.'

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he:
מזויף או פרוע. לכאורה תמוה דנאמן נגד השליש כשיש לו מיגו דמזויף ובאה"ע סימן קמ"א סעיף נ"ח פסק דאם אינו מקוים וטוען פקדון דאינו נאמן נגד השליש במיגו דמזויף. ונראה דשאני הכא דשם מש"ה אמרינן דהימניה שיהיה לגירושין אף אם ישקר ויאמר לגירושין אף במקום שיש לו מיגו דמזויף כיון דבמסירתו לשליש איכא למיחוש שמא יתן לה השליש ותלך ותנשא בו אף שאינו מקוים דהא יכולה להנשא אף באינו מקוים כמבואר באה"ע סימן קנ"ב ס"ט ועוד דהשליח יכול לקיים אותו כשיאמר בפ"נ ובפ"נ משא"כ הכא בשטר כשאינו מקוים איכא למימר דלא הימני' כלל דמאי היה לו לחוש דלמא ימסרנו להמלוה ויגבה הא לעולם יכול לטעון שדעתי במיגו דמזויף ואפי' שלא בפניו אנן נטעון מזויף ופרוע כמבואר לקמן. והנה בס' קצה"ח דימה שליש לנאמנות בסי' ע"א דלא מהני כשיש לו מיגו דמזויף דהוי כמיגו בענין הנאמנות עצמו וה"נ נגד השליש כשיש לו מיגו דמזויף דנאמן ולפי דבריו קשה דאם כן להנך דס"ל דאין השליש נאמן כשמכחיש השלישות א"כ כשאין עדים בשלישות לא יהיה השליש נאמן אפי' מודה בשלישותו דהא הוי ג"כ כמיגו בענין הנאמנות עצמו דהא יכול להכחיש השלישות ולו' דלא הימני' כלל. ובש"ס ובכל הפוסקים מבואר להיפך דהא בעל אומר לפקדון בגיטין השליש נאמן. ולפמ"ש הש"ך דמיירי בפקדון על תנאי כך וכך ע"כ מיירי בלא עדים דאי איכא עדים ליחזי עדים מאי קאמרי אע"כ דשליש שאני דעדיף מנאמנות דבמקום שהי, בידו לעשות כמו שאו' ע"כ הימניה ונתרצה שיהי, כמו שיאמר אפי' אם ישקר ומה מיגו שייך לזה דמיגו אינו אלא בירור שהוא אמת כמו שאומר ומה בכך שהוא אמת הא בגיטין גבי בעל אומר לפיקדון ג"כ איכא הוכחה דהבעל אומר אמת מכח אי אית' דלגירושין יהבי' ניהלי' לדיד' הוי יהיב ומ"מ אמרי' שהימני' אם שיהיה לגירושין אפי' אם ישקר ואפי' במקום עדים סובר הרשב"א דנאמן מטעם זה ומאן דפליג לא פליג רק במקום עדים אבל במקום מגו ודאי נאמן השליש כדמוכח באה"ע סי' קמ"א סעיף נ"ה וכנ"ל ודוקא כשאינו מקוים סובר המחבר דנאמן דהא לא הימני' כלל דמה היה ביד השליש לעשות דאם ימסרנו להבע"ד ג"כ יהי' נאמן לטעון פרוע. והנימוק"י והש"ך סוברים כיון דמודה שכתבו ע"כ היה יכול לקיימו בשום פעם והרי הימני' אפי' אם ישקר. אך הא ק' על הנ"י והש"ך דהא הא דאמרי' הימני' הטעם כיון שמסרו בידו נתרצה כמ"ש כיון שהי' יכול לעשות כן א"כ כשהשטר תחת יד הבעלים והיה יכול לקיימו בשעת מעשה רק שאח"כ מתו העדים והוא אומר פרוע קודם שמתו העדים נימא ג"כ הכי שנתרצה שיהיה כמו שיאמר המלוה כיון שהיה יכול לקיימו דמה"ת יהיה גרע מסירה ליד הבעלים מיד השליש ואין השכל סובל כלל שיהיה יד הבעלים גרע מיד השליש. גלל כן נראה דיש עוד טעם אחר בנאמנות השליש דהבעה"ת כ' הטעם בנאמנות השליש דמה שנתפרש לשני השליש הוי כאומר נאמן עלי אבא ומידק דייק ודמי לנאמן הדיין לומר לזה זכיתי ונאמן בעל המקח לומר לוה מכרתי דסי' רכ"ב וכ"כ המרדכי ש' התקבל ובתשובת מיימוני לס' משפטים סי' מ"ד בטעם נאמנות השליש בשלישותו בידו מטעם דמידק דייק וכ"כ רוב הפוסקי, הטעם משום דחזקה דאין אדם חוטא ולא לו. ולכאורה ק' דא"כ כל ע"א יהיה נאמן מטעם חוקה זו ועכצ"ל דכל ע"א חיישי' לאומר בדדמי כמ"ש התשב"ץ משא"כ בשליש דמידק דייק והטעם הוא כמ"ש הפ"י ריש גיטין גבי שליח להולכה דכל שהוא מחייב לעשות הדבר אמרי' ביה דמידק דייק א"נ כמ"ש הפ"י בקידושין גבי קדשתי את בתי דלא מהני חזקה זו דאין אדם חוטא רק להחזיק ולא להוציא מש"ה אינו נאמן רק שליש שיש לו קנין בהחפץ והוי להחזיק כמש"ל ומ"מ ק' דלמה להו לטעמים אלו ולא אמרו טעמא דהש"ס דהימני' דהיינו שנתרצה שיהיה כמו שיאמר אפי' אם ישקר כמ"ש התוס' בגיטין ובתשו' מיימוני סי' מ"ד אע"כ דכתבו טעם זה דנ"מ לנידון שכתב הנ"י בטוען פרוע ומכחיש השליש בשטר שאינו מקוים שאינו נאמן והוכיח דינו מהש"ס ובזה לא סגי הטעם דהימני' ונתרצה שיהיה כמו שיאמר אפי' אם ישקר כיון דאפילו במסרו לבע"ד דודאי הימני' מהני מיגו להכחישו ולכך כתבו הטעם דמידק דייק והוי כמו נאמן הדיין ונאמן בעל הפקח שכתב הסמ"ע בסי' רכ"ב הטעם דמידק דייק וכאלו האמינו חז"ל אפי, במקום מיגו ודין שני עדים ממש יש לו דאפי' יש לו מיגו הוי מיגו במקום עדים כמ"ש הרשב"א בחידושיו לקדושין גבי נאמן הדיין דאפילו יש לו מיגו לאמר לא קבלתיך להיות דיין מ"מ נאמן וכמש"ל בסי' כ"ג ומשה"נ לא מהני מיגו והחולקים לא ס"ל סבר' דמידק דייק מש"ה פסקו דמהני מיגו ולפ"ז העיקר כהנ"י והש"ך:
או פרוע עי' תומים שכתב דאם טוען פרעתיך אחר שהשלשתי בידך דאינו נאמן. דהא אינו נאמן לטעון פרוע רק במיגו דמזויף וכשיטעון מזויף יצטרך לישבע נגד העד דהא השליש אומר שאינו מזויף והוי משואיל"מ ודוק' כשטוען פרוע כשהשלשתי בידך שגם עתה מכחיש השליש נאמן במיגו. ולפענ"ד נראה דנאמן דאין זה בגדר מחוייב שבועה ואינו יכול לישבע נגד השליש מחמת שהשליש יודע שאינו מזויף דא"כ בכ"מ שיש שטר מקוים בע"א לא יהיה נאמן לטעון פרוע במיגו דמזויף משום דה"ל משואיל"מ א"ו דכל שאינו מקוים בשני עדים טענות פרעון בעצמו טענה מעליותא הוא מטעם שכתב הסמ"ע סי' מ"ו ס"ק ב' ועוד מקומות אחרים שאין מקומם כאן ויהיה הטעם איך שיהי' כיון דקיי"ל שיכול לטעון פרוע נגד שטר מקוים בע"א ה"נ נאמן נגד השליש וזה ברור:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en:
Forged or paid. At first glance this is difficult, for one should be believed against the third party when he has a migo that he could have claimed that the document was forged. Yet in Even HaEzer, siman 141, seif 58, it is ruled that if a bill of divorce has not been authenticated and the husband claims that it was deposited with the third party, he is not believed against the third party through a migo that he could have claimed forgery. It appears that the cases differ. There we say that the husband trusted the third party that the document should operate as a divorce even if the third party lies and says it was given for divorce, even where the husband has a migo of forgery. By placing the bill of divorce in the third party's hands, there is reason to fear that he may give it to the woman and she may marry on its basis even without authentication, because she may marry on the strength of an unauthenticated bill of divorce, as explained in Even HaEzer, siman 152, seif 9. Moreover, the agent can authenticate it by saying that it was written and signed in his presence. Here, however, an unauthenticated monetary document is different. We may say that the borrower did not trust the third party at all on this point, for what was there to fear? Even if the third party were to deliver it to the lender, the borrower could always assert payment through a migo of forgery. Even in the borrower's absence, beit din would raise the claims of forgery and payment on his behalf, as explained below. Ketzot HaChoshen compares a third party to an express credibility clause in siman 71, where such credibility is ineffective when the defendant has a migo of forgery, because the migo concerns the very matter of the credibility. He therefore reasons similarly that where one has a migo of forgery against a third party, he is believed. According to this, however, those authorities who hold that a third party is not believed when the very fact of the deposit is denied should also hold that when there are no witnesses to the deposit, the third party is not believed even where the depositor admits that there was a deposit. For here too the migo concerns the very basis of the third party's credibility, since the depositor could deny the deposit and say that he never trusted him. Yet the Gemara and all the authorities state the opposite, for in Gittin, where the husband says it was for deposit, the third party is believed. According to Shach, that case concerns a deposit subject to a particular condition, and necessarily there were no witnesses, for if there were witnesses we could simply hear what they say. Rather, a third party is different and stronger than an ordinary credibility clause. Wherever the matter was in his power to carry out as he says, the depositor necessarily trusted him and consented that the result should be as the third party states, even if he lies. What relevance does a migo have to this? A migo is only evidence that the party's present assertion is true, but even if it is true, that does not matter. In Gittin, where the husband says the bill was given for deposit, there is likewise evidence that the husband speaks truth from the reasoning that had he intended divorce he would have delivered it directly to her. Nevertheless we say that he trusted the third party that it should be for divorce even if the third party lies. Rashba even holds that for this reason the third party is believed against witnesses. Those who disagree do so only where witnesses contradict him, but in the face of a mere migo the third party is certainly believed, as is evident from Even HaEzer, siman 141, seif 55, and as stated above. The Mechaber holds specifically that where the document is unauthenticated the borrower is believed, because he did not entrust the third party with any effective power regarding it. What could the third party have done, when even if he delivered it to the creditor the debtor could still plead payment? Nimukei Yosef and Shach, however, hold that once the debtor admits that he wrote the document, he must at some point have been capable of authenticating it, and he therefore entrusted the third party even if the third party were to lie. Yet there is a difficulty with Nimukei Yosef and Shach. The reason we say that he trusted the third party is that by placing the matter in his hands he consented to whatever the third party could then accomplish. If so, when the document remained in the creditor's own hands and at the time of the transaction he could have authenticated it, but the witnesses later died, and the debtor claims that he paid before the witnesses died, we should similarly say that he consented that matters would be as the creditor says because the creditor once could have authenticated the document. Why should delivery into the hands of the owner himself be weaker than delivery into the hands of a third party? It is unreasonable that the owner's own hand should be weaker. It therefore appears that there is an additional basis for the special credibility of a third party. Baal HaTerumot explains that what was specified by both parties to the third party is comparable to their saying, "My father is accepted upon me as judge," and that the third party is careful and precise. It resembles the judge who is believed to say, "I ruled in favor of this one," and the seller who is believed to identify to whom he sold, in siman 222. Mordechai, in Perek HaTekabel, and Hagahot Maimoniyot to Sefer Mishpatim, siman 44, likewise ground the third party's credibility while the entrusted item remains in his hands on the fact that he is exacting in his recollection. Most authorities also explain it by the presumption that a person does not sin where he gains nothing. At first glance, if so, every single witness should be believed because of this presumption. Necessarily, we fear that an ordinary single witness may speak on the basis of an impression, as Tashbetz writes, whereas a third party is especially careful and exact. The reason may be as Penei Yehoshua writes at the beginning of Gittin regarding an agent for delivery: when a person is charged with carrying out the matter, we say that he is exacting. Alternatively, as Penei Yehoshua writes in Kiddushin regarding one who says, "I betrothed my daughter," the presumption that a person does not sin without benefit is effective only to maintain possession, not to extract property. A third party, however, has a proprietary hold over the entrusted object, and is therefore treated as maintaining possession, as explained above. Still, why were these reasons needed? Why did the authorities not rely solely on the Gemara's reason that the parties trusted him, meaning that they consented that the matter should be as he says even if he lies, as Tosafot in Gittin and Hagahot Maimoniyot, siman 44, explain? Necessarily, these additional reasons were written for the practical distinction addressed by Nimukei Yosef, where the debtor claims payment and contradicts the third party concerning an unauthenticated document. In that situation the reason of trust alone is insufficient. Even when a document is delivered to the creditor himself, whom the debtor certainly trusted in the ordinary sense, a migo can nevertheless defeat the document. Therefore they add that a third party is especially exacting and is comparable to the judge and the seller, whose credibility Sema in siman 222 explains on the ground that they are exacting. It is as though the Sages themselves gave him the force of two witnesses, even against a migo. A migo against such testimony is a migo against witnesses. Rashba writes similarly in his novellae to Kiddushin regarding the credibility of a judge, that even where the litigant has a migo that he could deny having accepted him as judge, the judge remains believed, as explained above in siman 23. For this reason a migo is ineffective. Those who disagree reject this special principle of precision, and therefore rule that a migo is effective. Accordingly, the principal ruling follows Nimukei Yosef and Shach.
Or paid. See Tumim, who writes that if the debtor claims, "I paid you after I deposited it with you," he is not believed. His only credibility to claim payment rests on a migo of forgery, and if he were to claim forgery he would have to swear against the third party, who testifies that the document is genuine. He would therefore be one who is obligated to swear but cannot swear, and must pay. Tumim distinguishes a claim that it was already paid when he deposited it, where even now he directly contradicts the third party and is believed through his migo. In my humble opinion he is believed even when he claims later payment. This is not within the rule of one who is obligated to swear but cannot swear merely because the third party knows that the document is not forged. Otherwise, whenever a document is authenticated by one witness, the debtor could never assert payment through a migo of forgery, because he would be unable to swear against that witness and would have to pay. Rather, whenever a document has not been authenticated by two witnesses, a claim of payment is itself a proper claim, for the reason stated by Sema in siman 46, seif katan 2, and elsewhere. Whatever the precise reason, since we rule that one may plead payment against a document authenticated by only one witness, the same applies against a third party. This is clear.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: פרוע. עיין ש"ך שהכריע כיון דהשליש היה יכול. לקיימו בשום פעם אע"פ שאינו יכול לקיימו עכשיו נאמן השליש וע"ב דהעיקר כהש"ך ואפי' טוען פרעתי אחר שהשלשתי נאמן ואם השליש כשר להעיד חייב לישבע נגדו ואינו יכול לטעון טענת השטאה או השבעה נגד השליש אפי' לא אמר א"ע. ש"ך:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: Paid. The Shach concludes that since the shalish at some point had the ability to validate the document, even if he cannot validate it now he is believed. The primary law follows the Shach. Even if the borrower claims, "I paid after I entrusted it to you," the shalish is believed. If the shalish is fit as a witness, the borrower must swear against him. The borrower cannot claim that his earlier admission was made in jest or merely to avoid appearing wealthy, even if he did not say "you are my witnesses."

pitchei_teshuva.he: אינו נאמן. ע' באר הגולה עד והכי נקטינן ודלא כהסמ"ע. גם הש"ך הביא דברי הב"ח אלו ומסיים וכן נראה עיקר. ועיין בת' מים חיים חח"מ סי' יו"ד שכתב ולפע"ד יראה להביא ראיה ברורה לדברי הסמ"ע כו' עש"ה:
pitchei_teshuva.en: He is not believed. See Be'er HaGolah, who concludes that this is the ruling, unlike the Sema. The Shach likewise cites the Bach and concludes that this is the primary view. See Responsa Mayim Chayim, Choshen Mishpat, siman 10, who writes that in his opinion there is a clear proof for the Sema's position. See there.

turei_zahav.he: (שם התובע ישלם שכר השלישות) כן העתיק הב"י בשם הגהות מרדכי וכ"ה בדפוסי' ישני' וז"ל רש"י היה מחייב לתובע לשלם שכר השליש כדאמרינן בב"ק מאן דכאיב ליה כאיבא ליזל לבי אסיא עכ"ל ותמהני דאין זה ראיה כלל ובסמ"ע נתן טעם שהיא לתועלת התובע והוא תמוה דמאי פסקא ואדרבא הא איהו ניחא ליה שיתנוהו לידו ולא לשליש ובהגהות מרדכי שנדפסו מחדש כתב שם שכר השליח וקאי אמ"ש בפרק ז"ב ואם הוצרך לשאול כותבין ושולחין וכו' וע"ז כתב שהתובע ישלם שכר ואע"ג דבסימן י"ד כתב המחבר בזה ששניהם יפרעו שכר השליח והוא מתשובת הרא"ש מ"מ הגהות מרדכי לא ס"ל כן ולפ"ז שפיר מייתי ראיה שם ובעיקר הדין בשכר שליש פשוט הוא מי שמבקש השלישות יתן השכר ומסתמא אמרינן שהוא לתועלת שניהם כנלע"ד ברור דנוסחא מוטעת היה לפני ב"י והרמ"א בהגהות מרדכי דלעיל:
turei_zahav.en: (Seif 4: The claimant shall pay the escrow fee.) The Beit Yosef cites this from the Hagahot Mordechai, whose old editions read that Rashi required the claimant to pay the escrow holder, relying on the principle that one who suffers pain goes to the physician. That is no proof. The Sema says the escrow benefits the claimant, but that is not necessarily so; the claimant may prefer direct delivery. Newer editions read “the messenger’s fee,” referring to the rule that if consultation is required, the question is sent elsewhere. In that context the proof is sound, although the Rosh holds that both parties pay the messenger. As for an escrow holder’s fee, the party requesting the escrow should pay; ordinarily it is presumed to benefit both parties.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he:
או פרוע כו' נראה בטוען פרעתי קודם שהשלשתי וא"כ מכחיש לשליש ושפיר י"ל מגו דהוה טוען מזויף דהוא דהוה מכחיש לשליש דהוי כע"א וא"כ הוי מגו להכחיש העד דהא אף בטוען פרעתי מכחיש לעד משא"כ אם טוען פרעתי אח"כ לא הוי מגו דמזויף דהוא מגו להכחיש העד דהרי שליש מעיד דמסרו בידו בחזקת מקוים אם לא שהוא קרוב או פסול:
פרוע כו' כתב הש"ך דנ"י כתב אם מודה דכתבו והוא ביד שליש א"צ לקיימו כלל וכתב לעיל דהוא דעת התו' ואני כתבתי לעיל דליתא דהתו' חולקים ויחיד היא הנ"י בדבר הזה דאף רש"י אשר בכוונתו מפרש הנ"י כן נראה דחזר בו דבב"מ פירש"י אין עליו עדים פירוש עידי קיום הרי דמפרש דאין על השובר קיום דנימא ביה לוה מקיים ולא מלוה רק שובר פשוט ולא פירש דאי אפשר לקיימו כלל ודלא תקשה רש"י להדדי נראה דרש"י פוסק כלישנא בתרא דר"נ הלכתא דבעינן דווקא מגו וכמו שכתיב בגיטין בשמעתיה בעל אומר לפקדון וכו' והשיגו התוספות שם על רש"י אבל רש"י סבירא ליה הלכה כלישנא בתרא וס"ל דלא סליק בתיובתא רק ס"ל הנך לישנא בתרא דמיירי דיש עליו עדים ולא עדי קיום וא"כ הא איכא מיגו ובסנהדרין דפריך מניה דהך בריתא הוא בס"ד דסימפון היוצא מתחת יד המלוה כשר וא"כ לא איירי כלל מעדי קיום וא"כ אין עליו עדים ע"כ עדי ממש ושפיר פריך אבל לבתר דאמרינן בגמרא דסמפון היוצא מתחת יד המלוה פסול וע"כ עדים דרישא היינו עדים קיום או שלינהו לסהדי וכו' א"כ אף סיפא מיירי דאין עליו עדים קיום ואיכא מגו ולא איתותב ר"נ כלל ולכך פסק רש"י כלישנא בתרא וא"כ לדינא ממש מעט אשר מצינו חברי' לסברת הנ"י בפוסקים ולית הלכתא כוותי':
urim_vetumim_tumim.en:
Or wildly, it seems to me that I have made a mistake before my wife and I deny the third and that the petitioner of the Holy One, who claims that he is falsely deposed to the third of his death, and that he does not deny that he is a third of them
Paid, and so forth. Shach cites Nimukei Yosef, who says that if the creditor admits that the receipt was written and it is in a third party's possession, there is no need to authenticate it at all. Shach wrote above that this is also Tosafot's view. I already explained there that this is incorrect. Tosafot disagree, and Nimukei Yosef is essentially alone in this formulation. Even Rashi, whom Nimukei Yosef understands as supporting him, appears to have retracted. In Bava Metzia, Rashi explains the phrase "there are no witnesses on it" to mean that there are no witnesses authenticating the receipt. This means the receipt itself is a normal written receipt but lacks validation; Rashi does not say that authentication is wholly unnecessary merely because it is in the third party's hand. The apparent inconsistency in Rashi can be resolved. Rashi rules like the second version of R. Nachman, which requires specifically a migo. In Gittin, Tosafot criticize Rashi for this, but that is his position. The second version need not have been conclusively refuted. It can interpret the baraita's phrase "there are witnesses on it" as meaning ordinary witnesses, not witnesses of authentication. Then the third party has a migo concerning an unsigned or incompletely evidenced receipt. In Sanhedrin, where the Gemara originally challenges from the baraita, the discussion initially assumes that a receipt found in the creditor's hand is itself valid. At that stage there is no question of authenticating signatures. Therefore, "there are no witnesses on it" necessarily means no actual witnesses signed the receipt, and the challenge works. After the Gemara concludes that a receipt found in the creditor's possession is generally invalid, the first clause must be reread. "There are witnesses on it" then means either that the witnesses themselves are present and confirm the receipt, or that the signatures have been authenticated. Correspondingly, the later clause concerning the third party can also mean the receipt lacks present authentication but the third party has a migo under the second version. The contradiction disappears. Thus Rashi can consistently rule like the second version of R. Nachman and still explain Bava Metzia as requiring authentication in the ordinary case. Practically, very few authorities support Nimukei Yosef's view that an unvalidated receipt in a third party's hands automatically needs no authentication at all. Since Tosafot do not actually say this and Rashi can be explained otherwise, the halachah should not follow Nimukei Yosef's lone position.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
שהוא מזייף דאין השליש נאמן יותר מאלו החזיר השטר לבע"ד עצמו וע"ז הימנהו ואם כן אלו מסר שטר ליד מלוה הלא יכול לטעון מזויף אם כן אף לגבי שליש נאמן:

אינו נאמן ואם הוא כשר להעיד דעת הסמ"ע דמ"מ אין חייב לישבע להכחיש העד דמצי לטעון טענת השטאה או השבעה כל כמה דלא אמר אתה עד והב"ח חולק דלא שייך טענה זו בשליש וכן הסכים הש"ך ונכון ועי' תומים ס"ק י"ג דכתבתי דאם טוען פרעתי במה דלא מכחיש לשליש אין נאמן במגו דמזויף ע"ש:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
He fakes one-third more loyal than those who have returned to the attorney himself and the High Court, and if so, it is a message that is not next to a companion who can’t claim fake if so about a loyal third:
Or wildly, he was a fake Dao Dao from all these places in a dirty hand and was faithful in the body of Dassssuf, with a third hand, and the same as the Dasssssel Lavah, was faithful to you:
He is not believed. If he is otherwise fit to testify, Sema holds that the litigant need not swear to contradict him, because the litigant can still claim that his earlier admission was joking or made merely to avoid appearing wealthy so long as he never said, "You are my witness." Bach disagrees and says those explanations do not apply to admissions involving an escrow holder. The Shach agrees with Bach, and this is correct. See Tumim, seif katan 13. If the litigant instead claims payment, in a matter where that plea does not itself contradict the escrow holder, he is not believed through a migo of forgery. See there.

שמת. פירוש ואנן טענינן ליתמי כל מה שאביהן הוי מצי למיטען. סמ"ע:
היתומים. ואם מת המלו' אח"כ גם בזה אמרינן דאין אדם מוריש שבוע' לבניו כ"כ הב"ח ופשוט הוא. ש"ך:
בקנין. דאז נשתעבדו נכסיו בשעת קנין וכותבין ללו' בלא מלו'. סמ"ע:
יתננו. כת' הסמ"ע בשם הטור דשני טעמים בדבר האחד שמא לוה בו ופרעו (פירוש והחזיר השטר ללוה) לפיכך נמצא בידו והפקידו החייב אצל זה והשני שמא לא לוה בו מעולם והתנ' עם העדים שיתנו השטר לידו ולא להמלו' ולא זכה בו המלו' כו' וגם לא יחזירנו ליד יורשי הלו' שמא אמר לעדים סתם קנו ממני לפלוני וכתבו לו השטר ונמצא שזכ' בו המלו' בהיותו ביד העדים ואפשר שטעו ומסרוהו ללו' שלא כדין עכ"ל. והש"ך הקש' על מ"ש דחיישינן שמא התנ' עם העדים כו' דלא זכה בו המלו' הא כת' הטור בס"ס ר"ן בשם אביו הרא"ש ז"ל דבמתנת בריא בקנין זכה המקבל מעת שהקנ' לו וא"צ שיגיע השטר לידו וכן מוסכם מכל הפוסקים וכ"פ הב"י בס"ס ל"ט דבשטר הקנא' לא בעינן דמטא שטרא לידיה כו' וצ"ל דשם מיירי שידוע שהקנ' בסתם בלי שום תנאי כגון שעידי הקנין הם לפנינו וכיוצא בזה וכזה תירץ הב"ח ע"כ והנה הש"ך השיג פה על הסמ"ע כמ"ש בכמה מקומות בסי' ס"ה ס"ב וס"ה ובסי' רמ"ג סי"ג ובסי' ר"ן סכ"ה ויען שחזר וכתבן במקומן לא רציתי להאריך כאן דוק ותשכח כ"א במקומו הראוי:
baer_hetev.en:
Died. It means that I will not answer everything that their father is, and that they will be saved. A:
Orphans. And if he died, then he said, “There is no man who is going to sleep for his son as a whole.” “Third:
in Cologne. Then his property was enslaved at the time of Kenan and wrote to Loj without a single. A:
He shall give it. The Sema writes in the name of the Tur that there are two reasons for the rule. First, perhaps the borrower once borrowed with this document and repaid it, meaning that the document was then returned to him, and for that reason it is now found in his possession; he subsequently deposited it with this person. Second, perhaps no loan ever occurred, and the borrower stipulated with the witnesses that they were to give the document to him rather than to the creditor, so the creditor never acquired rights under it. Conversely, the document should not simply be returned to the borrower's heirs either, because perhaps the borrower instructed the witnesses without qualification, 'Make a kinyan from me for so-and-so and write him the document.' In that case the creditor acquired the right while the document was still in the witnesses' hands, and perhaps the witnesses mistakenly delivered it to the borrower. The Shach questions the Sema's second concern, for the Tur states at the end of siman 250 in the name of his father the Rosh that with a gift by a healthy person made through kinyan, the recipient acquires from the moment of the kinyan and the document need not reach his hand. This is the consensus of the poskim, and Beit Yosef likewise rules at the end of siman 39 that a kinyan document need not reach the recipient. One must answer that there the kinyan is known to have been made unconditionally, such as where the witnesses to the kinyan are before us. The Bach similarly resolves the matter. The Shach repeats his objections to the Sema in several places, including siman 65, seifim 2 and 5, siman 243, seif 13, and siman 250, seif 25. Since he restates them in their proper places, Baer Heitev does not repeat them here.
