That the borrower came with him, and so forth. Sema explains that the borrower must actually come together with the third party because the borrower must know the terms of the entrustment and make a definite claim that the creditor delivered the note to the third party subject to those terms. If the borrower knows nothing except what the third party tells him, his uncertain claim is insufficient. Shach agrees. In seif katan 5 Shach likewise says that if a person gives a third party an object to deliver conditionally to another person, but that recipient knows nothing independently and relies only on the third party, while the giver denies ever appointing the third party, the object returns to its original owner. With an ordinary object, Shach's rule is clearly incorrect. Shach himself concedes that where the giver admits appointing the person as third party, the recipient acquires through the third party's statement even if the recipient personally knew nothing. The classic case, "the husband says for safekeeping and the third party says for divorce," concerns a woman who does not know what the husband said to the third party. This is evident from the later statement, "R. Huna concedes if she says, he gave it to him before me," which is presented as a different case. Yet in monetary law, or in another city where the "if it were so" argument does not apply, all agree that the third party is believed. Thus the recipient can acquire even without independent knowledge. Shach reaches his result only because he distinguishes between an owner who admits appointing a third party and one who says the item fell from him or was stolen. I have shown at length above that the primary view of Baal HaTerumot, Tur, and Mechaber does not generally suspect such loss or theft merely because it is asserted. Therefore, with an ordinary object, once the third party is believed, the recipient acquires through him even if the recipient knew nothing in advance. A loan document requires separate analysis. Suppose a creditor places his promissory note with a third party. Even if there were no note in existence at all, the borrower still owes the underlying money. Merely destroying or returning the note does not automatically forgive the principal debt. A creditor can say: "I waived my right to have a written loan or collateral, but I never waived the money itself." If the borrower admits he never paid, why should the third party's possession of the document extinguish the underlying oral debt? Similarly, returning collateral does not necessarily prove forgiveness of the principal. One might say the creditor surrendered the security while leaving the personal debt intact. Therefore, there is a strong reason to require the borrower to make a definite claim: "The creditor forgave the debt itself." If the borrower knows only from the third party, perhaps the third party's migo to burn the note proves only that the written lien is gone, not that the underlying money obligation was forgiven. Responsa Rosh, klal 68, indeed rules that where a third party says the creditor gave him the note to tear because he forgave the borrower, but the borrower himself says he did not pay and knows nothing of such forgiveness, the borrower must pay. Rosh adds that the third party is not believed because the creditor denies ever appointing him. I discussed that responsum above at length. Rosh's words imply, however, that if the creditor admitted making him a third party, the third party could be believed even to extinguish the principal debt. The reason is the entrustment itself. Why would the creditor hand the note to a third party with power to return it to the borrower? He knows the borrower could then boldly stand before him and say, "You were paid," relying upon possession of the cancelled note. By entrusting the paper in that way, the creditor accepted the third party's disposition and the consequences of the borrower receiving it. It is as though he accepted from the outset that the third party's statement concerning forgiveness or payment would govern. I have established above that we ordinarily do not distinguish between a creditor who admits the third-party arrangement and one who denies it through an implausible loss or theft claim, except in the special one-city situation governed by R. Huna's "if it were so" presumption. In the present case, where the document was deposited subject to a condition and there is a reason for using a third party rather than handing it directly to the borrower, that presumption does not apply. Therefore, the third party should be believed even if the borrower himself did not previously know the terms. This is particularly clear regarding collateral. Tur specifically added the case where the creditor sends collateral through a third party. If the third party is authorized to hand the collateral to another person or retain it himself, the creditor must realize that the borrower will not repay until the collateral is returned. By giving the third party that control, the creditor necessarily accepts that the debt can be treated as discharged under the stated terms. There is no meaningful distinction between collateral and another object conditionally entrusted for transfer. Thus Tur's addition of collateral reveals that he follows his father Rosh only in the special case where the creditor's denial of the third-party arrangement is supported by the "if it were so" reasoning. Outside that setting, the third party can determine even the status of the underlying debt. It therefore seems more likely that the phrase "the borrower came with him" is not a requirement that the borrower possess independent firsthand knowledge. Rather, it states an even stronger case. Even if the borrower comes together with the third party, creating an argument that "if the creditor truly intended to benefit the borrower, he should have handed it directly to the borrower who was right there," the third party is nevertheless believed. In monetary matters we do not automatically apply R. Huna's "if it were so" inference in this fashion. Sema himself in Perishah notes this possible reading, and I would add that it can even refer to a condition making it possible for the item ultimately to go to the borrower himself. One might think that because the borrower was present, the creditor's use of a third party is suspicious and supports the creditor's later denial. The ruling teaches that the third-party arrangement nevertheless stands. This likely reflects a disagreement with Rosh's stricter use of "if it were so" where the owner denies the entire entrustment. But as I explained above, many authorities, including Baal HaTerumot and Ramban, do not accept that concern broadly. Therefore, in my opinion, the borrower need not possess independent knowledge of the terms merely to rely on the third party. With an ordinary object this is clear. Even with a loan note or collateral, the better view is that where the third party's credibility is established and the factual setting does not trigger the special "if it were so" presumption, his statement can establish forgiveness or discharge of the underlying debt. The wording "the borrower came with him" should be understood as teaching the stronger case, not as a prerequisite for a definite firsthand claim.
And he should return it to the one who gave it. Shach writes that this applies where the agent has no migo. If he has a migo, he may deliver the item to the other person in accordance with the condition that was stipulated. I am puzzled by the underlying ruling of Rashba. Since an agent is believed regarding everything said to him when the matter was entrusted, as appears from the responsum attributed to Ramban, why should he not act according to the condition even if he was not formally appointed as the final third party? What difference is there between being believed because of a migo, as Shach says, and being believed because the parties trusted him? In either case his statement about the condition is accepted. Even if one argues that he was never authorized to carry out the condition personally, Shach's ruling where he has a migo is still difficult. His credibility does not itself appoint him judge or empower him to transfer another's property. At minimum, however, he should not return the item to the original giver before first stating the nature of the agency and its conditions before beit din. While he still has the item, he is believed concerning the arrangement. If he returns it first, his status may fall to that of a single witness and the other party can be harmed through his action. The correct explanation of Rashba's case is different. Reuven and Shimon had a joint debt against a gentile. Shimon handed the debt instrument to Levi to deliver it to Yehudah, who was to serve as third party, with a condition that if Reuven fulfilled certain terms the document would belong to him. Yehudah refused to accept the third-party role. Rashba therefore ruled that Levi must return the document to Shimon. The reason is not lack of credibility. Rashba holds that even where a formal third party receives a document, the person in whose favor the document is intended does not acquire it unless the giver says to the third party, "Acquire it for him." With a document whose transfer requires writing and delivery, even saying "acquire" may not suffice. Rashba discusses this at length in Responsa Torat HaBayit, siman 99. In the present case Shimon did not tell Levi to acquire the document for Reuven. He instructed Levi only to bring it to Yehudah, who would then hold it as third party. Since Yehudah refused, Reuven never acquired anything and Shimon remained free to retract. Levi therefore had to return the document. Accordingly, Shach's distinction based on migo is not correct. Even if Levi has a migo, Shimon may retract because Reuven never acquired the document. The ruling is limited to this type of case, where acquisition by the intended recipient still requires an act of acquisition. But if a creditor deposits a loan note with an intermediary on terms that if the borrower does such-and-such the debt itself is forgiven, no acquisition by the borrower is needed. The forgiveness operates automatically once the condition is fulfilled. In such a case the agent should not return the document to the creditor before stating the agency and its conditions to beit din, while his statement still has the full credibility of a third party. The same applies to any comparable case where the recipient's right arises without requiring the intermediary to acquire the item on his behalf. This is the correct practical distinction.
He should say it before witnesses. See Shach's discussion of Sema. Shach answers that if the third party goes before beit din, the judges may prevent him from handing over an item where the condition contains asmachta. Therefore he should make his declaration before ordinary witnesses instead. This is strained. If the law requires beit din to restrain him, he should go before beit din and they should act according to Torah law. It cannot be proper to avoid their supervision merely so that he can carry out the entrustment. The simpler explanation is that appearing before beit din is more burdensome than appearing before witnesses, as Shach himself notes. Here the case concerns a document whose payment obligations fall at different times. When the third party states before witnesses that the document was subject to a condition, the witnesses may write that statement without a special instruction to write, because their writing functions like a receipt. Below, siman 81, seif 29, we rule that witnesses may write a receipt without being expressly told to write. This is effectively a receipt that extends the payment time or records the condition affecting collection. By contrast, if the third party is returning money or an object and merely states before witnesses that the transfer is conditional, a written record prepared by those witnesses could later be used in beit din to extract property. That raises the problem of testimony from writing. Tosafot labored to explain why a written protest does not violate the rule against written testimony. Therefore, in that type of case one should state the matter before beit din rather than rely on ordinary witnesses to prepare a writing. This distinction resolves the language naturally.

שבא הלוה וכו' דעת הסמ"ע דווקא דידע הלוה וטוען ברי אבל אם לא היה במעמד השלישית ואין טוען ברי לא מהני ועיין תומים דהעליתי במשליש חפץ או משכון לית כאן ספק אף דלא ידע ממנו מכל מקום מהני השלישות ויעשה השליש כפי שלישתו רק במשליש שט"ח והלוה לא ידע אי גוף החוב נמחל בזו משמע גם כן מתשובת הרא"ש דאם השליש אמר החוב נמחל מכל מקום נמחל אף דלוה לא ידע וזה צריך קצת עיון ובפרט כשהמלוה מכחיש לשליש ע"ש. ומה שכתב שהלוה עמו לרבותא נקט ואפילו היה השלישית ראוי למסור ללוה וה"א אי איתא כדברי השליש למה לא מוסרו ללוה כיון דהיה שם במעמדו קמ"ל דלא ע"ש וסברא זו אמרינן בגמרא:
יעשה שליש מה שאמר לו השליח דהא השליח נאמן דהא היה לו מתחילה מגו ואם כן נאמן בכל דבריו מה שימסור לשליש והשליש נאמן כי כך אמר לו השליח ופשוט ולדברי הש"ך ה"ל לשליח מגו דאל"כ הא לא שייך הימנו בשליח כיון דמלוה מכחיש השליחות אבל לפי דהעליתי דאין נ"מ כלל בהכחשת השלישות אם כן אף דאין לו מגו דהא הימנ' מתחילה וכן מורי' דברי הרמב"ן שם בבעה"ת להדיא וכמש"ל:
ויחזור למי שנתן עיין תומים דהעליתי דמיירי בדבר דיכול המשלח לחזור בו עד שיזכה בו השליש עבור המקבל ולכך יחזור השליח למשלח אף דנאמן מכח הימני' דמשלח וגם יש לו מגו דמה בכך הא לא זכה בו המקבל ויכול משלח לחזור בו אבל בדבר דא"צ זכי' השליש כיון דשליח נאמן אין לו להחזיר למשלח עד שיאמר דבריו כהווייתן לפני ב"ד עכ"פ כדי שלא יפסיד למקבל כי נאמן הוא כ"ז ששלישתו בידו כמו שליש עצמו ע"ש:
השליש יעשה תמיד וכו' נראה דאיירי דאין שכנגדו מוחה עליו בב"ד אבל אם מוחה בב"ד פשיטא דאין לו להחזיר עד שיפסוק כפי הדין ובהכי ניחא מ"ש הרא"ש בתשובה כלל ע"ב דין ה' דהואיל דאיכא אסמכתא בשלישית לא יוציא השלישות מתחת ידו דשם מיירי דהוי מוחה ע"י בב"ד:
יאמר וכו' הסמ"ע הקשה דבס"ג מבואר דילך לפני ב"ד ותי' שלו וכן מ"ש ש"ך דחוק כמ"ש בתומים ולכן חלקתי ביניהם דכאן דה"ל להרחיב זמן שטר ה"ל כמו שובר וכשר מפי כתבם ולכך יכתבו עדים אבל בשאר שלישות להוציא לא מהני עדים דה"ל מפי כתבם ובעי ב"ד עיין תומים:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
When the borrower came, etc. Sema understands this specifically where the borrower knew about the escrow arrangement and makes a definite claim. If he was not present and has no definite knowledge, the arrangement should not affect him. See Tumim. I conclude that where an object or pledge was placed in escrow, there is no doubt at all. Even if the borrower did not know, the escrow is effective and the escrow holder acts according to its terms. Where a debt instrument was placed in escrow and the borrower did not know whether the underlying debt was remitted, Responsa Rosh also appears to indicate that if the escrow holder says the debt was forgiven, the debt is in fact forgiven even without the borrower's knowledge. This requires some study, especially where the lender contradicts the escrow holder. The Shulchan Aruch's phrase that the borrower "came" is therefore stated for added novelty. Even where the borrower was physically present and one might argue, "If the escrow holder's account were true, why did he not simply give it to the borrower while he was there?" the escrow holder remains believed. The Gemara itself uses this reasoning.
The escrow holder should follow what the agent told him. The agent is believed because originally he had a migo and could have acted directly. Therefore he is believed concerning the instructions he transmitted to the escrow holder, and the escrow holder in turn is believed to say what the agent told him. According to the Shach, the agent specifically needs that migo, because otherwise the principal's denial of agency would prevent us from saying the principal entrusted him. According to what I established above, contradiction of the escrow relationship does not change the result in this manner. Even without a current migo, the agent had been entrusted initially. Ramban's language in Baal HaTerumot explicitly supports this.
And he returns it to the one who gave it. See Tumim. The case concerns a matter in which the principal can still retract until the escrow holder acquires it on behalf of the recipient. Therefore the agent returns it to the principal. Even though the agent is believed because the principal initially entrusted him and he may have a migo, the recipient never acquired the item and the principal can retract. But where the transfer does not require a new act of acquisition by the escrow holder, once the agent is believed he should not return it to the principal until he at least states the true circumstances before beit din, so that the recipient not lose his right. So long as the item remained within his entrusted control, the agent has credibility comparable to an escrow holder. See there.
The escrow holder should always do, etc. This appears to speak where the opposing party has not protested before beit din. If he formally protests, the escrow holder certainly should not return or deliver the item until beit din rules according to law. This resolves Responsa Rosh, rule 72:5, which says that where the escrow arrangement contains an asmachta the escrow holder should not release the property from his hands. There the opposing party had already protested in beit din.
He should say, etc. Sema asks that seif 3 says the escrow holder should go before beit din. His answer, and the Shach's, are strained, as I wrote in Tumim. I distinguish the cases. Here the escrow holder merely has to extend the time of a debt instrument. That resembles a receipt, which can be established through valid written testimony. Therefore witnesses may write the statement. In other escrow matters where the testimony itself would extract property, ordinary written testimony does not suffice; the matter must be presented before beit din. See Tumim.

mechaber.he: אשה הנושאת ונותנת בתוך הבית ואפוטרופוס הממונה על נכסי בעל הבית (ומת בעל הבית) ויודעים שהיו לבעל הבית נכסים של אחרים והממון נשאר בידם ויודעים של מי הם חייבים להחזיר לכל אחד מהם שלו ואם לא החזירו ובאו לב"ד מהימנו במיגו:
mechaber.en: A woman who carries and is appointed inside the house and a guardian who is in charge of the property of the household owner (and the owner of the house) and knows that the owner of the house had the properties of others and the masses remained in their hands and knows who they must return to each of his own and if they did not return to the UN from our bodies:

baer_hetev.he: במגו. פירש הסמ"ע דאילו רצו היו מחזירים הממון לזה שאומרים עתה שהוא שלו וע"ל סי' ס"ב מ"ש דל"ת מזה וע' בא"ע סי' פ"ו מדינים אלו עכ"ל והש"ך כת' דלק"מ מסי' ס"ב דשם איירי מסתם אשה הנושאת ונותנת בתוך הבית ולא הי' הבעל מאמינ' בכל דבר וא"כ אין לה דין שליש אבל כאן מיירי באש' שהיא שולטת בנכסי בעלה בכל אשר לו ויש לה דין שליש מש"ה נאמנת ואפי' במגו דלמפרע דאיניש דעלמא לא מהימן מיהמנת איהי מה"ט וא"ל הא כת' המחבר כאן סתם אשה הנושאת כו' ולא ביאר דמיירי שהאמינ' והשליטה הבעל כו' י"ל מדכת' דין זה בסי' זה גבי דיני שלישות ולא קבעו בסי' ס"ב משמע דכונתו לומר דבאשה שיש לה דין שליש איירי וע"ש שהאריך להשיג על הסמ"ע וב"ח ושאר פוסקים בתשובותיהם מ"ש בדין זה וכת' עוד במי ששטר בידו ואומר שהוא שליש והטפסת השטר הוא ביד המלו' ומכחישו אם יש להשליש מגו שהי' יכול להחזירו בינו לבינו הוא נאמן ודלא כמ"ש בתשובת מהר"א ששון ע"ש:
baer_hetev.en: By virtue of a migo. The Sema explains that had they wished, they could have returned the money to the person whom they now say owns it. See further siman 62 for what he writes, so that no contradiction should be inferred from there, and see Even HaEzer siman 86 concerning these laws. The Shach writes that there is no difficulty from siman 62. There the case is an ordinary wife who conducts the household's business but whose husband did not entrust her with complete authority, and therefore she does not have the law of a third party. Here, however, the case is a wife who controls all of her husband's assets and whom he has trusted with everything he owns. She therefore has the law of a third party and is believed for this reason even with a migo relating to an earlier point in time, which an ordinary person would not possess. Although the Mechaber here speaks generally of a wife who conducts business and does not expressly say that the husband entrusted her with full authority, the placement of the ruling in this siman concerning third-party arrangements rather than in siman 62 shows that he is speaking of a wife who has the law of a third party. The Shach there extensively disputes the Sema, Bach, and other responsa on this subject. He further writes that if a person holds a document and says he is a third party, while a copy of the document is in the creditor's possession and the creditor denies his claim, then if the holder has a migo that he could privately have returned the document, he is believed, unlike Responsa Mahara Sasson.

beer_hagolah.he:
ש) תשובת הרא"ש תחל' כלל ס"ח מסי"ג
וכתב שם ואם ירא שאם יאמר הדבר ליורשים לא יחזירו הממון לבעליו חייב הוא להחזירו כדי לקיים מצות השבה:
beer_hagolah.en:
Responsa of the Rosh, beginning of rule 68.
And he said, “If he says it to the heirs, he will not return the money to his husband, he must return him to his watch.”

beur_hagra.he: אשה הנושאת כו' ואם לא כו'. סנה' ל"א ת"ר א"ל אחד כו':
beur_hagra.en: A woman who carries a quaint and if not. "Arise," he said:

chelkat_mechokek.he: ואין ראוי לעשות כן. כבר נתבאר לעיל סי' ל"ז סעיף ח' דאפי' בקדושין מצוה שלא יקדש בתו כשהיא קטנה עד שתגדיל ותאמר בפלו' אני רוצה:
chelkat_mechokek.en: There is no need to do so. It is already said above that he will not be blessed with his daughter when she is small until he grows up and says, “I want to do so.”

ketzot_hachoshen.he: אשה הנושאת. עיין ש"ך שהאריך והעלה דאש' הנושאת ונותנת בתוך הבית כיון דכל צרכי הבית הי' נחתכין על פי' והיתה שולטת בכל ממון בעלה ואם כן הימנה ולהכי אף על גב דהשתא לית לה מגו אפילו הכי נאמנת מדין שליש ועיין שם ולפי מ"ש לעיל בסק"א דבעינן גבי שליש שיאמר זכה בשביל שנינו ואם לא אמרו כן יכולין לחזור אם כן הכא נהי דהימנה במה שנתן לה כל אשר לו בידה מכל מקום הא לא אמר זכה בשביל שנינו ואפילו לפי מה שכתבתי שם דאתר שגמר עדותו הוי כגמר דין וא"י לחזור אפילו לא אמר זכה בשביל שנינו כאן כיון דהבעל מת ונכסי קמי יתמי רמי אם כן נתבטל ענין הנאמנות כיון דלא אמר זכה בשביל שנינו והיה יכול לחזור והא דאשכחן נאמנות השליש אפילו אחר מות המשליש היינו באומר זכה בשביל שנינו וכמו שכתב הרשב"א והגהת מרדכי דעיקר דין השליש מיירי בכהאי גוונא אבל אם הי' באופן שיוכל לחזור בו אם כן כיון דמת והי' היורשין יכולין לחזור אף על גב דלא חזרו בפירוש כי מת היינו חזרה וז"ב:
ketzot_hachoshen.en: A wife who conducts business. The Shach argues that a wife who conducts the household and all of her husband's financial affairs is like a shalish. Since the husband placed all his property under her control, he trusted her. Therefore even if she no longer has a present migo, she can be believed under the law of a shalish. According to what I wrote above, however, the central law of a shalish requires an arrangement in which the parties cannot retract, such as where they said, "Acquire on behalf of both of us," or where the shalish has already delivered his operative testimony. Here, although the husband trusted his wife by placing all his property in her hands, he never told her, "Acquire on behalf of both of us." During his lifetime he could have revoked her authority. Once he dies, the property lies before the heirs, and the personal arrangement of trust terminates. The heirs can stand in his place and revoke what he could have revoked. His death itself is effectively a retraction from an arrangement that had never been made irrevocable. The cases in which a shalish remains believed after the death of the person who deposited the matter with him concern an irrevocable arrangement, such as one where the parties said, "Acquire on behalf of both of us," as Rashba and Hagahot Mordechai explain. Therefore the wife does not automatically acquire the continuing credibility of a shalish merely because she had managed all household finances during the husband's life.

meirat_einayim.he:
ויודעים של מי הן פי' האשה והאפוטרופוס יודעים מש"ה חייבים להחזיר כו':
מהימנו במיגו דאלו רצו היו מחזירים הממון ליד מי שאומרים עתה שהוא שלו וע"ל סי' ס"ב סק"ז מ"ש דל"ת מזה ועיין בא"ע סי' פ"ו מדינים אלו:
meirat_einayim.en:
And they know to whom they belong. Meaning that the woman and guardian know the true owner. Therefore they are obligated to return the property accordingly.
From our place in Milo they wanted to return the crowd to those who now say that he is his and C. S. S. S. S. S. S. S. S.C. from this, and see the S.P.A. and these states:

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he: מהימנו במיגו. עיין בשו"ת רדב"ז סי' קמ"א דדוקא שאומרים של פלוני הם נאמנין אבל כשאומרים שחייב להם אינן נאמנין אם לא שאומרים שנתנו הבעלים להם רשות לפרוע וליתן להם משכנות אז נאמנים ובל"ה אינם נאמנים ולפמש"ל דברים פשוטים בטעמם דבשלמא אם אומר דבר זה של פלוני הוא הרשות בידו להחזיר להם ובדבר שהוא בידו נאמן אפילו להוציא דבידו הוי כשני עדים דאפילו בדבר שבערו' מהימני כמו בבעל שאמר גרשתי אבל כשאומר שפ' חייב לפלוני אף אם האמת כדבריו אין רשות בידו לתפוס משכון ולמסור ללוה דאף שיכול לתפוס במקום שאינו חב לאחרים מכל מקום אין לו רשות למסרו למלוה בלא רשות ב"ד ואין לו רק דין מיגו ומיגו להוציא לא מהני דכיון שהוא ברשות הנפקד הוי כמו ברשות המפקיד והוי כמו מיגו להוציא וכמש"ל בסמוך וכשאומרים של פלוני הם נאמנין אפילו לדעת הרא"ש בסי' ק"ח דכיון שהוא שולטת בכל אשר לו והוי כנותנו לו רשות להחזיר של אחרים ואם היא בעצמה לותה והקיפה משל אחרים שהיא בעצמה חייבת ודאי דהרשות בידה לפרוע ונאמנת לומר אפילו שחייבת לפלוני במיגו:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: They are believed through a migo. Responsa Radbaz distinguishes between saying, 'These items belong to so-and-so,' and saying, 'I owe so-and-so.' In the first case, one who controls the items is believed because he has authority to return them to their owner. What is in his power can function like two witnesses, even in matters of personal status. But if he says merely that the owner owes someone money, even if true he has no right to seize collateral and hand it over to the creditor without beit din. His statement therefore rests only on an ordinary migo, and a migo does not extract property where the item is legally still in the depositor's possession. If the owner explicitly authorized him to pay or to hand over collateral, then he is believed, because the act is within his authority. Likewise, where a wife or other manager says property is actually owned by another person, she can be believed where she had power over the property and therefore could have returned it. If she herself borrowed or incurred the debt and is personally obligated, she likewise has authority to repay and can be believed concerning that liability through the appropriate migo.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: במיגו. עש"ך דמיירי באשה שהיתה שולטת בכל אשר לו שנאמנת מדין שליש ובזה מיישב מה דקשה מכאן לסימן ס"ב ושם יבואר אי"ה) (וע"ב דדוקא כשאומרים של אחרים הוא גוף החפץ אבל אם אומר שהוא חייב לאחרים א"נ במיגו שהיו נותנין המטלטלין שלו למשכון אם לא שהן בעצמן הקיפו סחורה וחייבין בעצמן נאמנים וכתב עוד במי שהשטר בידו ואומר שהוא שליש והמלוה יש לו הטפסת השטר ומכחישו אם יש להשליש מיגו שהיה מחזירו בינו לבינו השליש נאמן דלא כתשובת מהר"א ששון:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: With a migo. The Shach explains this as a woman who controlled all of her husband's property and is believed as a shalish. That resolves the apparent contradiction with siman 62. See the Beurim: this applies when they say that the actual object belongs to others. But if the person says only that he owes money to others, he is not believed through a migo that he could have pledged his movables to them, unless they themselves extended merchandise on credit and are personally owed the money. If a person holds a document and says he is merely the shalish, while the lender holds a copy and denies him, then if the holder has a migo that he could have returned the original privately, the shalish is believed.

pitchei_teshuva.he: מהימנו במגו. עבה"ט עד והש"ך כתב דלק"מ מסימן ס"ב כו' אבל כאן מיירי באשה שהיא שולטת בנכסי בעלה בכל אשר לו ויש לה דין שליש כו' וע' בת' ושב הכהן סימן נ"ז דלא ניחא ליה תירוץ זה דאם כן היה לו להרא"ש לבאר חילוק זה ועוד דאם כן נתת דבריך לשיעורין וכתב לתרץ באופן אחר דבסימן ס"ב מיירי שאומרת או כתבה שמה שתח"י הם של אחרים היינו שהפקידו בידה או הלוו לה לכן אינה נאמנת לעולם אפילו יש לה מגו מטעם דהוה כאומרת שהם שלה דאינ' נאמנת אבל הכא מיירי שאומרת שהם של פלוני שהפקיד ביד בעלה או הלוה לו נאמנת היכי דיש לה מגו כו' וכתב ולפ"ז נראה פשוט דאין חילוק בין אם מסרה ליד ב"ד ואמרה בשעה שמסרה שהם של פלוני או אם מסרה ליד היורשים ואמרה אפי' שלא בפני ב"ד להיורשים כנ"ל ג"כ נאמנת. אבל אם מסרה סתם ולא אמרה אז רק אחר כך אינה נאמנת. ומ"ש הרא"ש בסוף התשובה והובא בב"י ואם יצא הממון מידה ובא ליד האפטרופס או ליד בית דין יעשו ב"ד ככל אשר תאמר האלמנה במגו כו' סתמו כפירושו שאמרה בשעה שמסרה שהם של פלוני והך ככל אשר תאמר אין לפר' ל' עתיד מה שתאמר אחר שמסרה אלא ל' הווה ככל מה שאומרת האלמנה ע"ש וע' בתומים ובנה"מ מזה:
pitchei_teshuva.en: They are believed through a migo. See Baer Heitev, citing the Shach's answer that there is no difficulty from siman 62 because here the case concerns a wife who controls all of her husband's property and therefore has the status of a third-party custodian. Responsa VeShav HaKohen, siman 57, is dissatisfied with this answer. Had this distinction been intended, the Rosh should have stated it, and the rule would become dependent on imprecise degrees of control. He therefore explains differently. In siman 62 the woman says, or wrote, that property in her possession belongs to others because they deposited it with her or lent it to her. She is never believed in that assertion, even with a migo, because it is functionally equivalent to saying that the property is hers, a claim for which she lacks credibility. Here, however, she says that the property belongs to a particular person because that person deposited it with her husband or lent it to him. In such a case she is believed when she has a migo. Accordingly, there is no difference whether she delivered the property to beit din and at the moment of delivery said it belonged to that person, or delivered it to the heirs and told them, even outside beit din, that it belonged to that person. In either case she is believed. If she delivered it without saying anything and only afterward made the claim, she is not believed. The Rosh's statement at the end of his responsum, cited by the Beit Yosef, that if the money leaves her possession and comes into the hands of the guardian or beit din, beit din should act in accordance with whatever the widow says through her migo, must be understood as referring to what she says at the time of transfer. 'Whatever she says' is present tense, not a future statement made after the transfer. See there, and see Tumim and Netivot HaMishpat.

siftei_kohen.he: והוא שלא יהיה ביניהם ובין השליש הכחשה כו' ואפי' יש עדים שעשאוהו שליש או ששניהם מודים שעשאוהו שליש מ"מ כשיש הכחשה ביניהם ובין השליש בסך הממון צריך השליש לישבע נגד התובע המכחישו וכמ"ש לקמן ס"ק י"ט ודלא כהב"ח סעיף א' ע"ש:
siftei_kohen.en: Provided that there is no contradiction between them and the escrow holder. Even if witnesses testify that they appointed him, or both parties admit doing so, if either party disputes with him concerning the amount of money, the escrow holder must swear against the claimant who contradicts him, as explained below in seif katan 19. This is unlike the Bach in seif 1.

turei_zahav.he: (סעיף ז') אשה הנושאת ונותנת. עמ"ש סימן ס"ב ועיין מ"ש סימן ק"ח סעיף ח':
turei_zahav.en: (Seif 7.) "A woman who conducts business." See what I wrote in siman 62 and in siman 108, seif 8.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he: אשה וכו' מקורו לקמן סי' ס"ב ושם בררתי הדברים ע"ש בזה בס"ד:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: A woman, and so on, came to C. S. S. S.C. and there I made it clear:
